title: Job 22:12–30
context: Eliphaz continues the same third speech, now moving from the charges of 22:5–9 to a picture of God in the heights, a claim that Job thinks God cannot see, a warning drawn from the fate of wicked men, and a call to return to the Almighty, lay treasure in the dust, pray, and be restored. These remain Eliphaz’s words, not the narrator’s verdict. Eliphaz attributes to Job a saying that God does not know and cannot judge through the thick darkness; Job has not been quoted in this book as saying those exact words, and chapter 23 will have Job say that he cannot find God, yet that God knows the way he takes. The call to acquaint himself with God and be at peace assumes that Job’s misery is the misery of an unrepentant man, which 1:1, 1:8, and 2:3 have not said. In 42:7 the LORD will tell Eliphaz that he has not spoken of God what is right, as his servant Job has; that later word belongs to the whole speech and is not restated in every verse. Both traditions read the unit as a friend’s counsel of retribution and repentance, to be heard as such, without a party contrast over the invitation itself.

verses.text: “Isn’t God in the heights of heaven? See the height of the stars, how high they are!
verses.arminianNotes:
Eliphaz asks, “Isn’t God in the heights of heaven? See the height of the stars, how high they are!” God is exalted, far above the earth. The thought will be used, in the next verses, to suggest that Job treats that height as a hiding of God, rather than as his majesty. The speaker is still Eliphaz.

Arminian readers take the height of heaven as a true confession Eliphaz makes, even while they wait to see how he will turn it against Job.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also receive the exaltation of God as right in itself, the stars as a measure of height, without yet granting the charge Eliphaz is about to invent.

Both traditions can share the confession that God is in the heights, and they keep the use of that confession as Eliphaz’s next move.

verses.text: You say, ‘What does God know? Can he judge through the thick darkness?
verses.arminianNotes:
Eliphaz claims that Job says, “What does God know?” and, “Can he judge through the thick darkness?” Eliphaz puts a question in Job’s mouth: that God does not know, and cannot judge through darkness. Job has spoken of God’s power and of his own confusion, but the book has not given these exact words as Job’s. The quotation is Eliphaz’s construction.

Arminian readers hear a friend’s misrepresentation, a charge of practical atheism that Job has not stated in this form.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also leave the quoted questions as Eliphaz’s report of Job, not as a line already spoken in Job’s earlier speeches, and not as the book’s summary of him.

Both traditions distinguish what Eliphaz says Job says from what the book has actually recorded.

verses.text: Thick clouds are a covering to him, so that he doesn’t see. He walks on the vault of the sky.’
verses.arminianNotes:
The invented speech continues: thick clouds are a covering to him, so that he doesn’t see, and he walks on the vault of the sky. In Eliphaz’s telling, Job thinks clouds hide God and that God merely walks the vault, unseeing. Again this is Eliphaz’s version of Job, and it should not be read as Job’s own theology already on the page.

Arminian readers take the covering clouds and the vault as part of the same attributed speech, a picture of a distant, unseeing God that Job has not owned in these words.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also keep the lines inside the quotation Eliphaz has begun in 22:13, a charge of a hidden, inattentive God, unendorsed by the narrator.

Both traditions refuse to treat this portrait as Job’s settled doctrine, and they invent no contrast over the image itself.

verses.text: Will you keep the old way, which wicked men have trodden,
verses.arminianNotes:
Eliphaz asks, “Will you keep the old way, which wicked men have trodden,” Eliphaz classes Job with an old path of the wicked, as if Job were choosing their road. The question is a warning and an accusation together, still in the friend’s voice.

Arminian readers hear Job being placed on a road he has not claimed, the “old way” of wicked men used as a threat rather than as a finding the book has made.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also leave the old way as Eliphaz’s comparison, a traditional path of judgment, not a proven description of Job’s life.

Both traditions keep the question in the friend’s mouth and do not make it the narrator’s path for Job.

verses.text: who were snatched away before their time, whose foundation was poured out as a stream,
verses.arminianNotes:
Those men, Eliphaz says, “were snatched away before their time, whose foundation was poured out as a stream,” The image is of a sudden end, a foundation washed out. Some readers hear a flood in the stream; the verse itself says a foundation poured out, and the notes do not assert a particular disaster beyond that wording.

Arminian readers take the sudden snatching as Eliphaz’s example of judgment on the wicked, offered to frighten Job into the next verses’ repentance.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also hear a traditional warning, a life ended early and a foundation gone like a stream, used in Eliphaz’s argument, not as an independent history the book has paused to tell.

Both traditions hedge any larger identification of the stream and refuse to build a reconstruction on it.

verses.text: who said to God, ‘Depart from us!’ and, ‘What can the Almighty do for us?’
verses.arminianNotes:
Eliphaz further describes them as those “who said to God, ‘Depart from us!’ and, ‘What can the Almighty do for us?’” The wicked are made to dismiss God. Eliphaz is still filling out the “old way,” and he is still implying that Job is near it. Job’s own speeches have been complaint and protest, not this dismissal.

Arminian readers hear a saying Eliphaz assigns to the wicked, not a quotation already taken from Job’s mouth.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also keep “Depart from us” as the voice Eliphaz gives to wicked men, a foil in his argument, not the book’s summary of Job.

Both traditions distinguish that dismissal from Job’s desire, soon to be spoken, to find God and come to his seat.

verses.text: Yet he filled their houses with good things, but the counsel of the wicked is far from me.
verses.arminianNotes:
Yet, Eliphaz says, “he filled their houses with good things, but the counsel of the wicked is far from me.” God had filled the wicked with goods, and Eliphaz separates himself from their counsel. The first clause admits that the wicked may be prosperous for a time, a point Job will press in chapter 24; Eliphaz turns it toward a moral distancing of himself.

Arminian readers note the admission of filled houses, and they hear Eliphaz’s “far from me” as his claim to stand elsewhere, not yet as a proof that his charges are true.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also let both halves stand in his mouth: God had filled those houses, and Eliphaz disowns their counsel. The later tension with Job’s catalogue of unpunished oppression is not settled here.

Both traditions keep the verse as Eliphaz’s, without a party contrast over the temporary prosperity of the wicked.

verses.text: The righteous see it, and are glad. The innocent ridicule them,
verses.arminianNotes:
“The righteous see it, and are glad. The innocent ridicule them,” Eliphaz pictures the righteous rejoicing over the fall of the wicked, with the innocent joining in ridicule. The tone is his. The book has not yet reached a scene in which Job is asked to take that stance toward anyone.

Arminian readers take the gladness and the ridicule as Eliphaz’s expected outcome of judgment, not as a command the narrator has issued to Job.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also leave the righteous and the innocent in Eliphaz’s sentence, a conventional close to the warning, unendorsed as the book’s ethic of gloating.

Both traditions report the lines without turning them into the book’s last word on how the righteous should look at the wicked.

verses.text: saying, ‘Surely those who rose up against us are cut off. The fire has consumed their remnant.’
verses.arminianNotes:
They say, “Surely those who rose up against us are cut off. The fire has consumed their remnant.” The quoted saying completes Eliphaz’s picture: the adversary is cut off, the remnant burned. Fire as the end of the wicked is his image here, not a scene the narrator has described in Job’s case.

Arminian readers hear a conventional boast of the innocent, used to press Job, and they do not take it as an account of Job’s own losses.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also keep the fire and the cut-off remnant as the words Eliphaz gives the righteous, a warning in proverb form, not the prologue’s story rewritten.

Both traditions refuse to identify Job’s disaster with this consuming fire as if Eliphaz had been given that reading.

verses.text: “Acquaint yourself with him now, and be at peace. By it, good will come to you.
verses.arminianNotes:
The appeal begins: “Acquaint yourself with him now, and be at peace. By it, good will come to you.” Eliphaz offers peace and good as the fruit of becoming acquainted with God now. The counsel assumes alienation caused by the sins he has named. It is not in itself a false invitation to peace with God, but it is aimed at a man the prologue has not called unrepentant.

Arminian readers hear a real call to be at peace with God, and they still reject the premise that Job’s need is to begin from proved wickedness.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also take the invitation as Eliphaz’s, peace and good promised on the terms of his diagnosis, which 1:1, 1:8, and 2:3 have not confirmed.

Both traditions can honor the desire for peace with God without accepting Eliphaz’s account of why Job lacks it.

verses.text: Please receive instruction from his mouth, and lay up his words in your heart.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Please receive instruction from his mouth, and lay up his words in your heart.” Eliphaz urges Job to receive God’s instruction and to store his words. The advice is pious in form. In this speech it is spoken by a friend who thinks Job has refused that instruction, and it should be heard in that setting.

Arminian readers take the call to receive God’s words as right in itself, and they do not grant that Job has been a man who would not hear them.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also leave the verse as a friend’s plea for instruction, good counsel in wording, still tied to Eliphaz’s unproven case.

Both traditions distinguish the worth of attending to God’s words from the accusation that frames the plea.

verses.text: If you return to the Almighty, you will be built up, if you put away unrighteousness far from your tents.
verses.arminianNotes:
“If you return to the Almighty, you will be built up, if you put away unrighteousness far from your tents.” Restoration is promised on return and on putting unrighteousness away. Eliphaz assumes there is unrighteousness in Job’s tents to put away. The conditional is his theology of this case, the same retribution already at work in 22:5–11.

Arminian readers hear a genuine promise of being built up in a return to the Almighty, and they still deny that the book has shown the unrighteousness Eliphaz requires Job to put away.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also keep the “if” as Eliphaz’s terms: return, put away unrighteousness, be built up. The later restoration of Job will not come on the basis of this diagnosis.

Both traditions refuse to treat the condition as the narrator’s verdict on Job’s tents.

verses.text: Lay your treasure in the dust, the gold of Ophir among the stones of the brooks.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Lay your treasure in the dust, the gold of Ophir among the stones of the brooks.” Job is told to put treasure and the gold of Ophir down in the dust and among the stones. Ophir is named as a source of gold, a place the book does not locate; the notes do not fix its site. The point in Eliphaz’s speech is renunciation of gold in order to have the Almighty as treasure in the next verse.

Arminian readers take the gesture as Eliphaz’s counsel of dispossession, aimed at a man already sitting in the dust, which gives the advice a harsh edge he does not seem to feel.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also hear gold laid in the dust as the friend’s prescribed surrender, Ophir left unidentified, the counsel still resting on the charges of 22:5–9.

Both traditions hedge the place-name and refuse to turn the gold into a symbol beyond Eliphaz’s contrast with 22:25.

verses.text: The Almighty will be your treasure, and precious silver to you.
verses.arminianNotes:
“The Almighty will be your treasure, and precious silver to you.” This is the promised exchange: the Almighty in place of gold. As a general sentence about God as treasure it can be heard with respect. In this speech it is the reward Eliphaz attaches to Job’s supposed repentance.

Arminian readers can receive the line as a true word about God as treasure, without accepting the path Eliphaz has marked for Job to reach it.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also let the Almighty be named as treasure, and they keep the promise inside Eliphaz’s offer, not as the book’s independent explanation of Job’s losses.

Both traditions distinguish the confession that God is treasure from the friend’s terms for obtaining him.

verses.text: For then you will delight yourself in the Almighty, and will lift up your face to God.
verses.arminianNotes:
“For then you will delight yourself in the Almighty, and will lift up your face to God.” Delight and a lifted face are promised after the return of 22:23–25. Eliphaz paints the end of Job’s quarrel as restored joy. Job’s next speech will be a desire to find God, mixed with terror, not this easy lifting of the face.

Arminian readers hear a beautiful promise, and they note that Eliphaz offers it as the simple sequel of repentance, which the following chapters will not follow in that form.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also keep the delight and the lifted face as Eliphaz’s expected close, a genuine good, still not a map the book has authorized for this moment.

Both traditions refuse to mock the hope of delighting in God, and they refuse to treat Eliphaz’s “then” as already the book’s timetable.

verses.text: You will make your prayer to him, and he will hear you. You will pay your vows.
verses.arminianNotes:
“You will make your prayer to him, and he will hear you. You will pay your vows.” Prayer heard and vows paid complete the picture of restored fellowship. Eliphaz speaks as if Job were not already a man who has prayed and offered (1:5). The notes do not turn this into a debate about whether prayer changes what God has purposed; they only report the friend’s promise.

Arminian readers take the hearing of prayer as a real hope Eliphaz holds out, and they do not grant that Job has yet to begin to pray.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also leave the verse as Eliphaz’s assurance that God will hear, a conventional restoration scene, not a new argument about the terms of prayer.

Both traditions keep the line in the friend’s speech and invent no contrast over it.

verses.text: You will also decree a thing, and it will be established to you. Light will shine on your ways.
verses.arminianNotes:
“You will also decree a thing, and it will be established to you. Light will shine on your ways.” Success and light are added to the promise. Eliphaz offers Job a future in which his word stands and his path is lit. It is the opposite of the darkness and floods of 22:11, still on the terms of 22:23.

Arminian readers hear an expansive pledge of established plans and shining ways, a friend’s picture of recovery, not a promise the narrator has made.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also keep the decree and the light as Eliphaz’s, a rhetorical heightening of restoration, unconfirmed as the book’s own pledge to Job in this moment.

Both traditions report the hope without making it a doctrine of Job’s coming authority.

verses.text: When they cast down, you will say, ‘be lifted up.’ He will save the humble person.
verses.arminianNotes:
“When they cast down, you will say, ‘be lifted up.’” Eliphaz imagines Job as one who can speak a lifting word when others are cast down, and he says that God will save the humble person. The second sentence is a general truth he attaches to Job’s supposed restoration. The first remains part of his offer.

Arminian readers take the saving of the humble as a right confession in itself, and they still hear the “you will say” as Eliphaz’s forecast, not as Job’s present office.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also distinguish the promise that God saves the humble from the role Eliphaz assigns Job in the first clause, a role hanging on the friend’s conditions.

Both traditions leave the verse in Eliphaz’s mouth and do not turn it into the book’s commission for Job yet.

verses.text: He will even deliver him who is not innocent. Yes, he will be delivered through the cleanness of your hands.”
verses.arminianNotes:
The speech closes, “He will even deliver him who is not innocent. Yes, he will be delivered through the cleanness of your hands.” Eliphaz ends with a claim that Job, once clean, would become a means of deliverance even for someone not innocent. The irony, in the book’s later movement, is sharp, but this verse is still Eliphaz’s promise, not the narrator’s scene in chapter 42. The notes do not read that later chapter back into the line as if Eliphaz had already meant it.

Arminian readers hear a closing pledge of wide deliverance through Job’s clean hands, a pledge that assumes the guilt Eliphaz has argued and has not proved.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also keep the not-innocent and the clean hands as Eliphaz’s last words, a friend’s vision of Job as restorer, not the book’s verdict spoken in advance.

Both traditions end the speech where Eliphaz ends it, still without treating his counsel as the book’s doctrine, and without a party contrast over the closing image.
